messages.mes:
The road took him along hedgerows and drainage ditches toward the walls, which grew as he walked—grey stone, taller than they had seemed from the verge, patched in places with newer masonry the color of old bone. Cart traffic thickened near the gate: a farmer with a wagon of cabbages, two men leading pack mules, a woman walking with a basket of chickens that muttered to themselves. The smell of the road was dust and animal dung and, underneath it, woodsmoke from the city's morning fires.

At the gate a queue of perhaps a dozen people shuffled forward between the towers. Two guards in the colors of the city watched the traffic with the loose attention of men doing an easy morning's work. One glanced at Alaric—staff, light robes, no wagon, no obvious trade—and waved him through with a jerk of the chin. Nobody asked his name or his business. Coin stayed in his pouch.

Inside, the noise came down all at once: wheels on stone, a smith's hammer somewhere to the left, a fish-seller crying her prices, voices overlapping in the local tongue that sat so naturally in his ears. The gate street ran straight for a short way and then split around a squat roundhouse, spilling into lanes in three directions. Laundry hung between upper windows. A dog scratched itself in a doorway.

Alaric stopped the first person who looked unhurried, a stout man in an apron dusted with flour, carrying nothing but his own opinions. The man listened to the question and squinted, taking Alaric's measure—the staff especially.

"Guild? Aye. Down this lane past the roundhouse, keep left where the road forks, and it's the big building with the green doors—you'll hear it before you see it, there's usually shouting. Quarter mile, no more." He shifted his weight and nodded up the lane. "That the way you're headed? Fine. Mind the cart rut halfway down, it's turned my ankle twice this season."

He went on toward the baker's without waiting for more.

The lane kept its promise. Past the roundhouse the road forked at a leaning signpost, and to the left, between a farrier's yard and a shuttered alehouse, stood a long building of timber and stone with double doors painted a deep green, flaking at the edges where weather had worked at them. He heard it before he saw it, as the flour man had said—a burst of laughter, then someone's voice raised in complaint, muffled through the walls.

He stepped over the cart rut halfway down without thinking about it.

Inside, the hall was broad and smelled of tallow, old leather and wet wool. A huge hearth burned low in the side wall. Long tables held clusters of armed men and women over breakfast and dice; a gallery ran along one wall plastered with notices and contract slips weighted at the corners. Nobody looked at him for longer than a glance. A boy with a stack of firewood pushed past toward the hearth.

The front desk ran along the right side, a counter of scarred oak with a low rail to keep the public back. Behind it sat a woman perhaps fifty, grey hair pinned up, reading a ledger. At Alaric's greeting she looked up, took in the staff and the robes, and closed the ledger with one finger holding his place.

"Registration, is it." It wasn't quite a question. She reached under the counter and produced a printed sheet and a small wooden case, setting both on the oak. "Simple enough. First time registering costs one silver—covers your measuring stone and your contract slip, both. You put your hand on the stone, it reads your Rank and Class, I write you into the branch roll, and you're an F-rank member with a slip to show for it."

She tapped the sheet. "Name goes in the book. Guild doesn't ask where you came from, but it does record who you are. That's the whole of it. Coin now, hand on the stone after."

She slid the case a little closer to the rail and waited.

"Better." The two coins vanished under her palm and into the till drawer without ceremony. "Alaric. Single name?" She was already writing as she asked, quill scratching down the roll's page. "Fine, single name it is. Plenty come through here with less than that."

She turned the wooden case toward him and lifted the lid. Inside sat a flat grey stone the size of a hand, worn smooth at its center where years of palms had rested.

"Hand flat on the stone. Don't squeeze it, it's not a weapon. It reads what's in your blood, takes a breath or two, then it's done."

Alaric laid his hand on it. For a moment there was nothing but coolness under his palm and the clerk's steady eyes. Then a faint warmth rose through the stone, and a thin line of pale light moved beneath its surface like something swimming under ice, and went still again.

The clerk leaned over, read the stone's surface, and made a small sound in her throat.

"F rank, Mage Class. Level one." She wrote it into the roll in a businesslike hand, then reached under the counter again and produced a small rectangular plate of dull grey metal, stamped with the Guild's mark and a fresh set of notches for rank and standing. She set it on the counter beside the case, next to his hand. "There's your plate. F-rank Novice, Alderwatch branch. Keep it on you—desk checks it, some clients want to see it, and if you lose it there's a fee to cut a new one, so don't."

She blew across the wet ink of the roll and closed it.

"That's you registered. Now." She folded her hands on the ledger. "Contract slips are on the board behind you, and F-rank work's the bottom row. Delivery, culling, watch assistance—nothing that'll eat you, mostly. Take what you fancy to the desk here, I'll make it active, and bring back proof when it's done. Payout's at this desk, fixed sum, no haggling." She glanced toward the hearth end of the hall. "Any questions, ask now, or ask the board."

messages.mes:
The ferry road ran south out of Alderwatch beside the river, packed dirt and old cart ruts, busy enough at this hour with a hay wagon, two women driving geese, and a boy leading a mule loaded with split firewood. The morning had warmth in it already, and the river smelled of mud and green water.

A mile down, a tinker with a handcart pointed south with his chin before Alaric had finished asking. "Flats? Keep the river on your right till it spreads. Can't miss the weirs—poles and fish traps all through the channels."

The road narrowed after that. Alderwatch dropped behind its own walls, and the country opened into low meadow, then marsh. The water began to split and wander, braiding through wide beds of reed that hissed in the light wind. Stakes stood in the shallows in long rows, and nets hung from frames to dry, and the smell shifted from river mud to fish and tar.

The first fisher he met was knee-deep in a channel, hauling a trap. He straightened when he saw the staff and the contract slip held up, and called to someone farther out.

"Warden's man, is it? Or Guild?" He waded closer, water sheeting off his leather apron. "Guild, then—good. They've not launched a boat in four days." He pointed down the braid of channels, where three low boats sat tied at a rough jetty and a handful of fishers stood about on the pilings with their arms crossed, doing nothing and visibly hating it. "Weirs run out that way, half a mile of channels. Striders took the far stretch two days back—four, we counted, maybe more in the reeds. One of ours got a cut across the arm before they pulled out."

He wiped his hands on his apron. "They're quick in the reeds and they come at the boats from under the waterline. Anything else you want from us before you walk out there?"

messages.mes:
The fisher waded back to his trap and left him to it.

A narrow causeway of packed peat and old planks ran out between the channels, just wide enough for one man, and Alaric took it with the staff in hand. The reeds stood taller than his head on both sides, and the sound of the jetty fell away behind him until there was only wind in the reeds, water lapping at the weir stakes, and his own footsteps on the boards. Here and there a trap hung off a frame, and one hung torn, its wicker split open and empty.

Half a mile was longer on a narrow causeway than on a road. The channels braided and rebraided around him. Twice he passed marks that were not fishers' work: long grooves dragged up over the peat, wet-gleaming, each about a finger wide, in sets of four, running from the water onto the bank and back in.

The far stretch announced itself by what was missing. The weir stakes here stood bare—no traps, no nets—and the nearest platform, a low deck on pilings where a fisher would normally work a line, had a coil of rope lying unraveled across its boards as if someone had left in a hurry.

Then the reeds stopped hissing.

Off to his left, thirty feet out in the channel, one of the things stood half above the waterline among the stalks, and it was watching him. A bog strider stood taller than a man but wrongly, all stilt legs and low slung body, its hide the grey-green of wet reed sheath, four limbs planted in the shallows with the front pair ending in hooked claws. It did not move. Water ran off its jaw.

And because the reeds were no longer hissing anywhere, because the whole flat had gone quiet at once, it was a fair guess the other three were close by and likewise still, somewhere under the surface or in the green walls on either side of the causeway.

The one in the channel shifted its weight, and a slow ripple ran out from its legs.

messages.mes:
He went forward along the planks, staff up, watching the water on both sides.

The dead strider drifted out behind him, and the channels ahead lay still. Grooves crossed the peat more often now, four-toed drag marks stitched everywhere between the weir stakes, and one of the low work platforms had a claw score raked clean across its deck, pale wood showing through old grey. The reeds hissed in the wind and told him nothing.

Past the second bend the causeway narrowed where a channel had eaten into it, and there the story of the place sat plainly: a sunken eel boat, half under, its prow wedged in the stakes, lines trailing slack in the current. Not fresh. The wood had greyed.

Then the water off to his right bulged.

It came up out of the channel without a splash, a strider surging out of the reeds ten feet ahead of him, water sheeting off its body, front claws swinging up over the causeway edge as its stilts drove it up onto the planks. It was on him before the first one's charge had even left his memory, and its hooked claw came down toward him across the narrow boards.

At the same moment, from the left, a second pair of stilts came fast through the shallows behind it, reeds parting in a long line.

He put the second lance into the smoking one.

The bolt went into the ridged breastplate where the first burn had already split it, and this time the plate gave. It toppled across the narrow causeway with a crash that jarred the whole frame, half its long body hanging over the torn edge into the sunken boat below, and did not move again.

His arm shook. The staff's tip guttered faintly, and his reserves felt scraped close to the bottom, the fire in it thin now, a few good casts at most.

The strider shifted its weight, stilts flexing.

messages.mes:
Dagny grunted something that might have been thanks, and the cart rolled on. Alaric passed through the Westgate on foot with the queue thinning around him—guards who glanced at the bloody sleeve and looked away, the press of the gate market just inside, fish and bread and a knife-grinder's wheel shrieking. He crossed the square by the shortest line he could manage and took the lane behind it, and from there he knew the way as well as his own boots.

The Guild hall was cool and dim after the sun, smelling of lamp oil and old parchment. Same clerk at the desk, woman about fifty, same ink-stained fingers. She looked up, and then she looked at him properly—at the arm cradled against his chest, the dried blood down to his wrist—and set down her pen.

"You went out this morning," she said. It wasn't a question.

Alaric put the contract slip on the counter. The seal on it showed READY, and she read it, then read him again, and something in her face shifted from clerkly indifference to a moment of plain arithmetic: one man, four striders, walking back in.

"Well." She took up the slip, touched it to the ledger, and the seal dulled as it settled into the roll. "Cull contract, complete. Ninety copper." She counted it out onto the counter, two short stacks, and pushed them across. Then she stopped, pen hovering over the ledger, and looked at the arm again.

"That needs a healer before tonight. There's a Temple bench behind the gate market—white door, red lamp, they'll want coppers you now have." She nodded at the coin. "Sit down first, though. There's a bench by the wall."

The hall was quiet around them. A pair of adventurers at the far table went on arguing over a map, and nobody else looked up.

messages.mes:
The coin clicked into his pouch and the bench took him. It was plain planking against stone that held the day's cool, and he sat with the staff propped between his knees and let the hall go about its quiet business around him—the map argument rolling on without reaching anything, a courier dropping a sealed satchel, the clerk's pen scratching. The arm throbbed in time with his pulse, no worse, no better. Ninety copper sat against his hip and four striders didn't.

When he stood, the walk back through the gate market was shorter than the walk out had felt. The knife-grinder was still shrieking. The lane behind it was narrow and shaded, and the white door stood where Dagny and the clerk had both put it, a red lamp burning above it even in daylight, its glass smoked with age.

Inside was one long room, warm from a stove, smelling of clean linen and something bitter boiled. Two benches, a partition, and a heavyset woman with grey hair braided tight who looked up from rolling bandages. Her eyes did the same arithmetic the clerk's had, but faster, and ended somewhere further.

"Sit down before you fall down," she said, nodding at the nearest bench. She came around the partition, took his arm in both hands without asking, and turned it toward the light. The sleeve was stiff with dried blood; she clicked her tongue at it the way Dagny had clicked her tongue at the mule.

"Deep, and it's been open since morning." She was already reaching for shears. "This comes off, and the stitching will hurt, and it'll cost you. Ten coppers the needlework, two more for the salve and the wrapping." She glanced up at his face, shears poised at the sleeve. "You'll live either way. Your coin, your call."

messages.mes:
"Twelve." The shears went through the sleeve from cuff to elbow, and the cloth peeled away wet. She looked at the bite for a long moment, then at his face, at the grey under his skin, and her manner changed—no more clicking, all business now. "You've lost more than you think, boy. Sit back. Don't be stubborn about it."

She worked fast. The needle went in and he felt every pass, hot and dragging, but her hands were steady and sure, pulling the edges together with short deft stitches while the stove ticked and the bitter smell of the salve rose up. Halfway through she tipped a cup of watered wine at him without looking. "Drink. All of it."

He drank. She tied off the last stitch, packed the line with salve that burned and then cooled, and wound the bandage tight from wrist to below the elbow, tucking the end in with a practiced thumb.

"There. Keep it dry, come back in eight days for the thread out. If the flesh goes red past the bandage or starts to smell, you come back sooner." She wiped her hands and held the other out for the coin, and he counted twelve coppers into it—two stacks and two over, the way the clerk had paid him.

She weighed it in her palm and finally looked at him properly, not at the wound. "Whatever you fought did this and you're still standing. Sit there another quarter hour before you walk anywhere." She nodded at the bench. "The stove's warm and I don't charge for sitting."
